analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear argument now in two cases that have been consolidated for argument. Number 97, 1927, Rodney C. Hanlon et al. versus Paul W. Berger. And 98, 83, Charles H. Wilson versus Harry Lane. Mr. Cordray. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. I represent the Marshal Service officers in Wilson and all the officials in Hanlon. There are two issues in these cases, the constitutional issue itself and the further issue of whether, in any event, these officers should be held personally liable for money damages when, at the time they acted, the law was not clearly established and it was not apparent that their conduct violated the Fourth Amendment. We submit that however the Court decides the constitutional issue is a matter of first impression in this case, Mitchell v. Forsythe compels the result that qualified immunity should be upheld for these officers here. Turning first to the constitutional issue, as framed by the Court, the issue is whether law enforcement officials violate the Fourth Amendment when they permit members of the news media to accompany them in order to observe and report on their execution of a warrant. We submit that it would be wrong to erect a per se rule that in all circumstances such conduct is improper, certainly to the extent that the search in the Hanlon case involved open fields or had the arrest of Dominic Wilson occurred in a public place. It would be unproblematic that the media accompanied the officers and observed and reported on their execution of a warrant. As a larger matter, moreover, there are many instances throughout this country every day in which third parties accompany officers as they execute warrants, and this has been true since the inception of bench warrants. There are many different circumstances. They may be there to join in performing the search or the seizure in assistance of the officers. They may assist the officers in other, more tangential ways, provide clerical help, translating, identifying evidence. They may also help facilitate the law enforcement objectives that are served by procuring and implementing the warrant itself. Well, let's get to the help that you claim was provided here. What's your argument here? Your Honor, as reflected in the Justice Department policy in the U.S. Attorney's Manual, in effect at the time of the Hanlon search and — It has since been — that section has since been repealed? Since been amended. That's correct. Yes. Amended out of existence, as I recall. No, modified. Modified with respect to the execution of a warrant. How does it read now? It still is the case. This is set forth in the appendix to the blue brief in the Hanlon case that law enforcement offers may assist the news media in reporting on and observing and video — Does it say that they may take members of the media into people's houses, into private places? It doesn't speak to that, but it has now specified that they should not facilitate media accompaniment in the execution of a warrant, Your Honor. However, at the time, the policy certainly countenanced such conduct and, in fact, encouraged it. However, the purposes served are the same ones that were served as stated in that policy, which are to promote the aims of law enforcement by deterring criminal conduct and by enhancing public confidence. Well, why do you have to take photographers into someone's house to aid law enforcement in that respect? I mean, you can have a news conference when it's over if you want to. I don't see why you have to take people into private places. Well, this Court has held that the Fourth Amendment doesn't require a least intrusive means test as long as the conduct is real. No, I just want to know whether there's anything substantial to this or whether it's fluff. Well — It sounds like fluff. Well, certainly, Your Honor, to the extent that the media are permitted to give a firsthand objective account of the actual events, that facilitates accurate reporting on law enforcement functions, and it may be quite helpful in preventing abuses in instances. But why just the media, Mr. Cordray? Do you know of any other area of law in which the media, quotes, have been given special constitutional privileges that John Q. Public wouldn't have? No, Your Honor, and no one contends that the media should have special privileges here. So they could have brought in maybe their sister-in-law to watch the thing, too, as well. Is that it? Many law enforcement departments around the country do have a public ride-along program that will permit public to ride along with officers and observe — Is it ride right into the house? Yeah, right into the house or inside premises on a search warrant? Or is the program more one of letting them ride in squad cars and see whatever occurs on the street? Well, there are a variety of such programs, and I'm sure that in various circumstances — Do you know of any that allow private citizens to accompany officers inside dwellings to execute a search warrant? Yes, Your Honor, the Marshal Service policy at issue in the Wilson case in place at the time clearly countenanced page 7. No, but your argument was that there were — throughout the country, there was a practice of ride-along, and our question is, do they ride right into the house? Yes, Your Honor, we have — Do you have specific instances in which this is going? We have cited to the court the Fletcher case from the Florida Supreme Court, which recognized as a matter of common usage and custom at the common law as of 1972 that it was common practice to allow media to accompany police even into private property or residence. Excuse me. I think the question that we're pursuing is, are individuals other than those in the media going into people's houses for the execution of warrants in a capacity simply as observers, not performing any law enforcement function? And I think we got the — several of us, I guess, got the suggestion from you that the answer to that was yes, and we want to know whether that is specifically correct. Is there a practice out there in the country, apart from the Marshal Service, of taking members of the public performing no law enforcement function into private places during the execution of a warrant? That's where I beg to differ. The purpose of a public ride-along program, as with a media ride-along program, is to serve law enforcement purposes. That's the whole — it's not merely for someone's entertainment buyer to set up. All right. We'll accept that qualification. Are members of the general public going into people's houses during the execution of the warrants? Is this a common practice? We'd just like to know that. I can't speak to that one way or another, Your Honor. Do you have any instances? I can speak to the fact that it was recognized at the common law as of 25 years ago that it was common practice around the country for media to a company. For media to a company, but not for private individuals. As far as you know, it is not and has never been common practice for police officers to bring in non-media people to show that everything's open and above board. I can't speak to that one way or another, Your Honor. Can you answer my question? As far as you know, there was no such practice. I believe that's right. I wouldn't want to concede that entirely. Do you know of any such practice? I know that there are public ride-along programs. I'm sure they have different components. I don't know for certain that they contemplate entry into a home, but they do contemplate public attending and something else. Can I ask you specifically about the law school programs? There are law schools that do have their students ride-along. Indeed, some of them have had professors who have written books about their ride-along experiences. Are there controls on that kind of ride-along to avoid the unnecessary intrusion on people's privacy? I'm certain that they are just as a matter of common-sense practice and to avoid potential lawsuits and the like. I can't firsthand speak to law school programs around the country, but I do believe that they are fairly common. In the Montana case, there was no entry into the house by virtue of the warrant. Isn't that true? That's correct. There was no execution of the warrant in the home. The only entry into the home was accompanying Mr. Berg with- By consent. By consent to explain the situation to his wife so there wouldn't be a misunderstand. But there was an entry into sheds and outbuildings, as I understand it. Correct. With regard to those, does the evidence disclose whether those buildings had open doors or anything like that? Or what do we know about those sheds and outbuildings? The search in the Hanlon case was executed in two different places, in open areas on the ranch, which I think fairly clearly would fall within the open fields doctrine, although it is private property, and at the same time in outbuildings. And the record, as far as I can tell, does not disclose for certain one way or the other whether they were within the curtilage or not. But there may well be, I think there is a constitutional argument, that they are open fields. That issue wasn't resolved below because it was pretty much a per se rule applied, I take it. I think that's right both ways, by the district court in our favor and by the Court of Appeals. Do you understand the open- We don't really know whether open- whether sheds, closed sheds at least, that are outside the curtilage come within the open fields doctrine. We haven't held one way or another on that point, have we? I don't believe the Court has specified all the details of that. No. Well, you don't understand the- or maybe you do- the open fields doctrine to permit a police officer to stay on an open field if the owner tells them to leave, do you? As I understand the open fields doctrine, it would because the Court has said that searches of open fields, even though they may be private property, do not implicate the Fourth Amendment. And therefore, I think that that's correct, although, again, I don't believe the Court has specifically announced that. In the Oliver case, the Court was referring to the fact that the officers happened to be in an open area and they were concerned with viewing something in an open field from a highway. Right. But in this case, the police and the accompanying news people demanded, in effect, entrance and had the right to enter under a warrant. Well, that's correct. And threatened the owner with imprisonment if he obstructed their search. It seems to me that's quite different. I'm not sure the open fields doctrine would apply if you told the police officer to leave. I think it's an open factual issue in this case. And I think what's germane to the issue that the Court has framed is that there was no execution of a warrant in a home in that case. And if this Court is particularly concerned with execution of a warrant in a home, that would not be implicated on the facts of the handling case. Well, supposing there's a policeman that's standing out on your front lawn and you tell him, get off, and he says, no, I want to look in your window. I mean, is that a trespass violation or a Fourth Amendment violation or what? Well, as here, the police are operating pursuant to a valid warrant, and it's been determined in both cases that they were properly executing the warrant. In a situation where the police are looking through a window, they may or may not have a right to be at the vantage point they're at. But I think that bears on the open fields question. It may. It may. And, again, I think that's an open factual issue. Why do you need a warrant under the open fields doctrine? I think you would not need a warrant, although perhaps in an abundance of caution to avoid any problems that might arise in later litigation or motion to suppress, certainly the better practice would be for the police to obtain a warrant, as they did here. But in any event, to return to the Constitution — Of course, just because the police can play around in open fields, it doesn't mean that they can bring along anybody else they want to play in the open fields. No, but certainly — So, I mean, even if you resolve the open field question, there's still the further question of whether whatever open fields immunity from the Fourth Amendment the officers have extends to the officers bring along somebody else as well, I assume. I think that's correct, but that's why I thought it was important to emphasize that the Court should not erect a per se rule against media company in all circumstances where a warrant is involved. In many instances, a warrant will be executed in such a way as to not even implicate Fourth Amendment interests. It might be executed in a public place. It might be executed in an area of open fields. Certainly the nature of the intrusion is much reduced in that setting. And across the board, across the spectrum, at different possible settings, each of them somewhat fact-specific, each of them raising maybe a greater or lesser extent of intrusion, those are factors that would be relevant in trying to draw this balance. But as you put it, we should adopt a rule regarding media accompaniment. So it is part of your case that there's a different rule for media and that it's better to bring media along than to bring your sister-in-law. I think it's more beneficial in certain respects and it's more of a concern in certain respects. Personally, I'd rather have your sister-in-law along. Perhaps. The Court framed the issue in terms of media, but in general, the Court has never addressed the issue of any third parties coming along. We don't contend that the media have a special privileged constitutional right of access. They do not under this Court's cases. But they, as surrogate for the public, could potentially be there should not be discriminated against. It's not as though the media should be the one individual not permitted to do what private individuals might otherwise be permitted to do. It's fairly common, isn't it, Mr. Cordray, to bring along the claimant to stolen property with a search so that it's his property, presumably, if they are successful, and he should identify it? Yes, Your Honor. There are a variety of practices where third parties are permitted to accompany police and have been thought to be, without problematic discussion, reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. But those are to aid in the specific search, not for some more systemic purpose of criminal administration. In many cases, that's true, but there are also a number of instances in which that really can't be maintained. For example, in the Hanlon case, the assistant prosecutor, Chris McLean, accompanied the officers. It wasn't contended that he was helping to execute the particular search, but he was there serving the same objectives for which the officers had sought and obtained a search warrant in the first place to enforce the federal wildlife laws. He was probably going to be prosecuting any charges that might be brought in. It was thought it would be useful for him to attend and observe the execution of the warrant. Well, wouldn't there be some purpose, too, to take along someone who is a lawyer in case you run into some uncertain Fourth Amendment situation? Can you go ahead and break down this door, or should you get a warrant or something like that? I think that certainly would be reasonable, although it's not contended that that was the case here in this case. But, again, I think what's important is, under Michigan v. Summers, is that the Court needs to apply a reasonableness standard. I think that's agreed among the parties here. The specific requirements of the Fourth Amendment don't speak directly to this other than the reasonableness laws. And it's a balance between the nature of the intrusion on the one hand and the objective served by the practice on the other hand. Well, does it then all boil down to the value that the media provide to law enforcement when they go into the House? Is that the nub of the case? I think that's an important factor. That's what we have to value against the privacy intrusion. I think that is the one side of the balance in all of these cases. The other side of the balance may change. It may be of greater concern or lesser concern in various circumstances. But I think that's correct, Your Honor. That would be the balance. You say here that the value of having media coverage of this particular execution of a search warrant outweighs the privacy interests of the ranchers who were searched. Again, we think in the Hanlon case that's correct, in particular because they were merely searching outbuildings in open areas. There was a search that did not involve criminal conduct that appeared to involve any intensive privacy matters. Well, let's assume for the moment, since it hasn't been decided, that some of these outbuildings were within the curtilage and, therefore, the same rules would apply as to the home itself. Now, how do you weigh that balance if it involves that? Let's say a search of the home. All right. I think that the fact of entering a residence is obviously an important consideration. It is a consideration that raises the nature of the intrusion and magnifies it. So certainly that's a concern. On the other hand — How do we weigh the balance where maybe there is, in some broad sense, a value to having public information about it, but, on the other hand, is a very weighty interest on the part of the homeowner to have privacy within the home? Yes. We have valued that very highly. That's correct. So how do we weigh that balance, in your view? In our view, we would suggest that in any case where we're talking about execution of an arrest warrant, not involving a search that's going to be into private papers or personal effects, we can pretty much adopt a general — But inside the home. That's right. That execution of an arrest warrant is going to be generally reasonable to allow media company because an arrest is a public event. Well, but I didn't pose arrest warrant. I pose, which is involved in the other case, a search warrant for items executed in the home or within the curtilage. I think that it's fairly clear that as we proceed along a spectrum here, a search warrant in the home is more problematic than an arrest warrant. I think it's more problematic than a search of outbuildings, certainly more problematic than a search of open fields. Yes, and that would — Could I pursue the value to law enforcement that having the media along is? You say it's in assistance of law enforcement. I assume that means to assure that everything is open and above board, that they're not being brutal, that they're not exceeding the limits of their authority. Is that right? That's certainly much of it. I think also there is the — What is it beyond that other than PR? Well, the PR itself is very important. I mean, it certainly helps to deter criminal conduct for people around the country to know that the officers are aggressively pursuing crime. Criminals often think they're not going to be caught. If they know that the officers are aggressively pursuing crime, they may think twice before they — Just photographing them going into the building, saying these officers are, you know, going in and they're going to do a search. Do you have to be there while they're opening dresser drawers? No, not necessarily. And, again, that has to do with the nature of the intrusion. But at any alone — It seems to me the principal value you're appealing to is the value of making sure that law enforcement is conducted fairly and properly. Nobody has a greater interest in that than the person being searched. So why don't you just ask the person before you bring in the television news crew, you know, we're going to do you a favor to make sure that this search is going to be absolutely fair. We have a television crew along. Would you like them to come in to be sure that this search will be very fair? They could do that, and certainly they could seek — It seems to me they ought to, if that's the principal value of — Perhaps, but it's not a silly — it's not a silly point. It's not — it shouldn't merely evoke laughter. I mean, it's not as though police know ahead of time that they're going to commit an abuse or they're not going to commit an abuse. They deal with unforeseen circumstances and having a third-party president may well defer a — My point is why don't you ask the homeowner if he wants that protection? Why force it upon him when he'd rather — he trusts the police force and values his privacy more? They certainly could do that. In various cases, perhaps they should do that. Whether they are obliged to do that in all cases, I guess, is part of the calculus. I suppose, too, that some sort of photographic present might uphold the validity of the search against complaints by the person who's being searched. In fact, that was true in the Hanlon case here. Are there no photographers other than those in the media? Couldn't you bring along — I thought there were police photographers. There are police photographers. They may or may not be available. It might be within the discretionary officer to decide, gee, we have a photographer here through this means. That might be the best way to execute it on the spot. Typically, those decisions have been left at the discretion of officials who must implement these policies. I take it you're not arguing here that the photographers were brought along because there was no available police photographer. We don't know that one way or another. Again, as a matter of objective reasonableness, the fact that their photographs or videotape could be used, as in Hanlon, they were used to resolve the consent issue, may be, again, a part of the calculus. Mr. Gorda, as I'm listening to your argument and you keep saying no per se rules and it depends on what the particular facts and circumstances are, I have a certain deja vu feeling and it relates to the old days when this court was trying to draw a luggage line, telling the police they couldn't search the green suitcase but they could search the paper bag. And then finally they decided in Ross, no, the police have to know going in what they can do and what they can't do. And your argument seems to me to be going back to the time when, well, we'll decide after the fact and there'll be no rules going in. Isn't there some real importance to being able to tell the police in advance what's okay and what isn't? Yes, Your Honor, I think there is. And as I say, this Court has never addressed this whole general area of who can come with police, and so some guidance will be useful in this case. But to draw bright lines at the outset in a reasonableness balancing area might or might not be prudent. Here I think there are certain bright lines that could be drawn. Any time an arrest warrant is being executed, I think in general it will be objectively reasonable to permit media to accompany observe. If a search warrant is being executed not in a residence, in an outer area, I think per se that probably will be acceptable to allow accompaniment. If you have a search warrant in a home that's going to involve rummaging through private papers and personal effects, perhaps you could determine that it's a general matter that might well be unreasonable. I think there's some areas where it clearly would be unreasonable. Any search involving a physical invasion of the body, body cavity search or the like, just as the number of officers present at such a search is always minimized, I think any third party being present would be per se unreasonable. Now, we also have an issue, I guess, in the Hanlon case concerning audio tapes that were made while the officers and the media were in the House? Correct. There was an audio tape made of what discussion occurred as Mr. Berger and the officer were speaking to Mrs. Berger. That's unproblematic. Should we make any distinction between audio tapes and video tapes? I don't think so, Your Honor, but certainly audio tapes have been directly addressed by this Court in terms of the cases of people wearing a wire, the White versus the United States, Lopez more recently, Cacheres, in which the Court has ultimately found there's not a constitutional problem when an individual is speaking to a government agent, even if they don't know that person to be a government agent. Here, by extension, they knew full well they were speaking to Federal agents. I don't think there could be a reasonable expectation of privacy in those conversations. As to whether the Court — So far, your argument so far lays the groundwork for you to talk about the second question, which is whether or not these principles were clearly established. Perhaps you could address that. Sure. Thank you, Your Honor. The Mitchell v. Forsythe case on qualified immunities on all fours with this case, there there was an allegation that the Fourth Amendment was violated. It was a wiretapping case. At the time of the actions, there were only two Federal decisions, both unpublished, which had upheld the legality of such conduct. It was a fairly common practice. It had been occurring episodically for 25 years. Well, the Fourth Amendment doesn't talk specifically about wiretapping, but it certainly talks about houses and personal effects. That's right. And eventually, in the Keith case, this Court ultimately resolved that such conduct was unconstitutional. But the decisions that held that post-dated the events in question in the Mitchell case. All of that is on all fours with this case here. The only decisions at the time here had indicated that such conduct was — Isn't there a distinction between going into somebody's home and wiretapping? I mean, going into people's homes has been something considered questionable under the common law going for many, many years. That's correct, Your Honor. There is legal precedent that certainly makes that a harder issue in this case, and depending on how the Court rules, it may become clear now that this practice is unacceptable. Do you think we can charge the officers with knowledge of Semaine's case or the principal in Semaine's case? Yes, although we've indicated that Semaine's case is quite distinguishable in our brief. In Semaine's case, it was service. That's the British case involving service of civil process in a home, and the Court itself distinguished between civil process and criminal process, which it said the public safety supersedes the private. Blackstone echoed that, and that's generally been this Court's approach. For example, in Payton, recognizing that an arrest warrant permits an intrusion into the home. So, again, I think to extrapolate from older, especially British cases and early cases, general principles to say that officers must have known how those apply in these specific instances would be harsh, particularly given that the courts that had attempted to apply such principles had found that this conduct was constitutional. And the only decisions that have ever been cited to the contrary post-dated these events. Moreover, if this were an unusual practice, if it had not been engaged in, except very occasionally around the country, that might explain the lack of this. How frequently it's done. You rely heavily on the marshal service policy. Not only that, Your Honor. Well, you do rely on that heavily, do you not? We do, but the Fletcher case — Well, let me just ask you a question. Yes, sir. Can you point to me the part of the policy that makes it clear they could take people into the homes? I didn't find that in what this cited for me. Page 7 of the joint appendix in the Wilson case contemplates that there may be occasions. It says, if the arrest is planned to take place inside a house or building, agree of head time on when the camera can enter and who will give the signal. That isn't an express authorization in all circumstances to take media into a home, but it certainly contemplates that a rule that would say you can never allow the camera or the media — Well, I thought the sheriff, the Montgomery County sheriff, in his deposition testified that permitting civilians to enter a home during the execution of a warrant wasn't permitted there. That was his view, and that may be his policy. There are a variety of policies around the country. I think it's important — Well, that might have been clearly established, at least in Montgomery County. Well, I don't think so, given that the case law at the time did not clearly establish it, and judges since have disagreed, you know. And this was a practice that was common. And we point to the Fletcher case from the Florida Supreme Court, which recognized this as a common practice of common law as of 1972. And the Prawl case on remand at trial court in Wisconsin found this to be a common — Well, in Wilson v. Lane, the facts were pretty extreme in terms of an invasion of privacy in the home. It occurred in the early hours of the morning when the couple were asleep and were not, you know, adequately dressed. I mean, it was an amazing invasion. And you think, on that balance, that we would not be concerned about the privacy interests in that situation simply because it was an arrest warrant? I think certainly the Court would be concerned. I think the fact that it's an arrest warrant weighs in the balance. Do you think we should have a clear rule that in executing an arrest warrant, you can take outsiders in who aren't there to help with the execution of the arrest warrant? I would tend to suggest a more fact-specific approach to these cases, but if the desire is to draw some bright lines, that may be one that could be — That might be a very easy, clear line to draw. Could be. If I could reserve the remainder of my time, Mr. Vettel. Very well, Mr. Cordray. Mr. Fletcher Hill will hear from you. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. There are two fundamental facts that establish the qualified immunity of the three deputy sheriffs I represent. The first of those is that the most able lawyer researching this issue in 1992 would have found no cases from any court condemning the mere presence of media when a warrant is executed lawfully as a constitutional violation. The only cases then in existence, in fact, held to the contrary, that media presence at most was a tort under common law principles if the media was brought inside a home. The second point is — May I ask on that, Craig? Suppose it had been clearly established that it was a common law tort to bring the media into a home, but there had been no decision on interpreting Section 1983 of the 14th Amendment. Would you think under those — under that assumption there would be qualified immunity? No, Your Honor. I think it would still be an open question whether the — whether this Court would eventually incorporate those common law principles into the Fourth Amendment. Well, assume that — assume that we — and the first time we get — we decide, yes, it's a clear violation, that the only issue we have to face is should the officers have been aware that they shouldn't go in if their only restraint on going in was a well-established common law rule — a common law tort rule. No, because the doctrine of qualified immunity would operate only as to the constitutional principles. There may be other immunities for the officers concerning the common law, and, in fact, one could find the situation where the common law would suggest to these officers that they should not do this. But as a matter of Fourth Amendment jurisprudence and the Bivens or 1983 action against the officers, I think the law would still not be clearly established as a matter of constitutional principle. Don't you think it's a clearly established constitutional principle, that it is unreasonable to commit a tort in the course of the search? I mean, once you — I mean, I think it's an open question of whether it was clear that this was a tort. But if it was a tort, I think the game's up. Surely you're not authorized to commit a tort in the course of a search. No, Your Honor. Wouldn't that make the search automatically unreasonable? Do you need a case that says that? Let me give an illustration. The technical issue of trespass may be such that, in the absence of a warrant, something would clearly be a trespass. But if the officer is in the position under Fourth Amendment jurisprudence of having authority to come into the House based on a warrant, then that potential superior authority of the officer would overcome the tort violation. Well, supposing you have, during a search or an arrest, an officer commits what's later decided to have been an assault and battery. You run up against the person in a way a court says there wasn't — that that wouldn't make it invalid under the Fourth Amendment, would you? That's correct. You would still have the issue under the Fourth Amendment of whether that use of force, which might admittedly be a battery at common law, is justified by the need to control under Michigan v. Summers the people who are in the premises where the warrant is being executed.
